projects.summary: For Bad Bunny’s DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOToS World Tour, All of it Now served as the Disguise media server programmers and Notch artists for a production built around an approximately 10,000-pixel-wide camera-driven canvas. The team developed cinematic Notch looks alongside custom CRT and VHS tools, a hybrid pipeline incorporating physical analog VHS processing, and a real-time Unreal Engine motion capture system that brought Bad Bunny’s character Concho to life onstage.
projects.title: BAD BUNNY

children.text: For Bad Bunny’s DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOToS World Tour, All of it Now served as the Disguise media server programmers and Notch designers for a production that evolved into a fully camera-driven system across an approximately 10,000-pixel-wide screen surface. The show ran for nearly three hours, requiring a large library of real-time looks that could maintain both visual impact and performance across the full canvas.

A major focus of the real-time development was recreating the tactile characteristics of analog media within the camera system. AOIN developed custom Notch tools to reproduce the distortion, texture, tracking, and other imperfections associated with CRT and VHS formats. The pipeline also incorporated physical VHS processing, allowing analog footage to be routed back into the real-time system and composited alongside the digital treatments. This combination of physical and digital processing gave the camera looks, creating a more authentic analog character than a purely simulated approach.

The production also featured a real-time motion capture system built around Bad Bunny’s character, Concho. AOIN developed the character creation and rigging pipeline in Unreal Engine, along with the real-time facial capture system used to drive the digital character during the show. The captured performance was translated directly onto Concho in real time, allowing the character to interact with Bad Bunny during the interstitial rather than relying on pre-rendered animation.

Together, the camera system, custom analog processing, and Unreal Engine mocap pipeline created a set of real-time tools capable of supporting very different visual requirements within the same production. The result was a camera-driven show that combined large-format Notch content with physical analog processing and live digital character performance.

projects.summary: For Rauw Alejandro’s *Cosa Nuestra Tour* in early 2025, All Of It Now worked alongside STURDY. providing show programming, render farm services, and equipment rentals. The technical package included GX media playback servers supporting the show’s content and playback infrastructure.
projects.title: RAUW ALEJANDRO

children.text: For Rauw Alejandro’s Cosa Nuestra Tour in early 2025, All Of It Now worked alongside STURDY. across show programming, media server operation, render farm services, and equipment rentals. The show featured an approximately 45-track setlist, including interstitials, with the full production programmed and operated on GX media playback servers. This included supplying and building the show playback structure, programming content and cues, and managing the media server system throughout the live production to ensure the large-format content ran reliably across the tour’s 4K+ wide screen surface.

Supporting the content pipeline was a dedicated nine-server render farm running Deadline 10. The system provided both 3D rendering through Cinema 4D and 2D rendering through After Effects, processing high-resolution content for final Notch LC outputs. Two staff members supported the render farm on a rotating basis, maintaining continuous 24/7 coverage throughout the production. Together, the programming, live operation, media server rentals, and rendering infrastructure provided a complete technical workflow from content delivery through final playback on the touring system.

writeupBlocks.text: RAUW ALEJANDRO needed content that could carry a full arena show and still feel live — not a video playing behind the artist, but a stage that responds in the moment.

The brief was a stage that could change character between songs without a hard cut — so the content had to be generative rather than baked, reacting to timecode and to the band on stage instead of running as a fixed film.

We built the look as a set of real-time systems in a single scene graph: camera-aware grading, particle fields tied to the low end, and a set of LED-native transitions that never resolve to a seam. Playback ran redundant, with a warm spare tracking the show frame-for-frame.
Everything was authored to survive the tour: one operator, a fixed I/O map, and content that degrades gracefully if a panel drops rather than tearing the whole surface.

projects.title: MARTIN GARRIX

children.text: For Martin Garrix’s Americas Tour, All of it Now worked alongside PHNTM and Creative Director Gabe Fraboni across content production, real-time Notch camera systems, system engineering, equipment, and the development of a volumetric LED system. The project combined a large-scale content pipeline with custom real-time and touring infrastructure designed to carry the production across both the North American tour and concurrent festival run.

The content pipeline evolved throughout development, with the scope expanding beyond the initial brief and requiring multiple rounds of deliveries. Each delivery cycle introduced new visual material and reveals throughout the tour, allowing the show’s content package to continue developing as the production moved into the summer festival season.

Alongside the rendered content, All of it Now developed more than 35 unique Notch camera looks for the show. The treatments ranged from camera-driven effects to more substantial compositions, creating a real-time visual system that complemented the rendered content while responding directly to the live performance.

A major component of the project was the development of the volumetric LED system surrounding the stage. All of it Now designed the playback architecture, hardware, and content pipeline required to operate the grid, integrating the system into the broader visual production rather than treating it as a standalone display. The team also created more than 100 pieces of volumetric content designed to be busked throughout the show, giving the operator a flexible library of visuals that could be triggered and layered in response to the performance.

From a touring systems perspective, All of it Now designed, fabricated, and delivered the primary server rack for the Americas Tour, along with a dedicated festival flypack. The touring system marked the first deployment of Disguise X2 in a touring environment, while its licensing model allowed the same software licenses to be utilized across both the full-scale touring rack and the portable laptop based festival system. This provided a consistent software environment as the production transitioned between the North American tour and festival configurations.

The result was a flexible production infrastructure connecting rendered content, real-time Notch, volumetric visuals, and custom hardware across the full touring cycle, with the flexibility to introduce new content and live visual elements as the production evolved.

children.text: For Peso Pluma’s Dinastía Tour in 2026, All of it Now developed a real-time previs system for STURDY. to accurately represent the show’s automated stage systems. AOIN also provided screens production support throughout the content pipeline, helping connect the creative development with the requirements of the live production.

A major component of the project was the development of Notch camera looks used throughout the entire show. The system covered every song, with treatments ranging from subtle enhancements to the live camera feed through to full-screen compositions that made the camera the primary visual source. This allowed the visual language to shift significantly from song to song while maintaining a consistent real-time system across the production.

PSN tracking was integrated into the visual pipeline to connect the content directly to the automated LED doors within the stage design. Position data from the stage automation could drive visual elements in real time, allowing the content to remain aligned with and respond to the physical movement of the doors. This created a direct connection between the stage automation and the visual system rather than treating the two as separate production elements.

By combining real-time previs, screens production, Notch camera systems, and PSN tracking, the project connected the show’s content and physical automation throughout development and into the live production. The Dinastía Tour went on to sell out every show.

projects.summary: For *Fallout*, a large-scale virtual production workflow integrated tracked cameras, real-time Unreal environments, and 2D plates within a 24K LED volume. Working alongside Satore Studio, the team developed custom tracking and visualization tools while managing complex multi-camera workflows throughout the production.
projects.title: FALLOUT

children.text: Fallout is one of the most beloved and longest running video game series of all time, and has now been beautifully adapted for television by visionary creators Jonah Nolan and Lisa Joy.

The Fallout series is a masterclass in executing the full potential of a transmedia project. The show leverages assets from the games, which establish a clear dialogue with the original IP, and features expansive environments, creatures, and rich worldbuilding, along with virtual production technology in new and exciting ways.
AOIN Involvement

All of it Now collaborated with longtime partner Satore Studios to assemble a uniquely knowledgeable virtual production team that could realize its complex workflows. The AOIN team’s background in developing cutting-edge workflows on the fly allowed them to build tools that facilitated collaboration between multiple departments with minimal prep time, which is a hallmark of live event production. The team’s ability to also translate that mentality to TV and film production proved virtual to the project’s success.

All of it Now’s background in live-show production and integration of real-time technology tools proved vital to the project's success. Developing tools that enable multiple departments to collaborate cohesively on set with minimal prep time is a hallmark of live event production, and translating that mentality to TV and film production is a unique skill.

For this production, All of it Now was responsible for managing multiple tracked cameras, over a dozen render nodes, and 8 roaming LED carts that were all tracked within a 24K-resolution 90’ by 75’ LED volume designed and engineered by Fuse Technical Group.
Technical Challenges
Part of what made filming Fallout so SPECIAL was its use of celluloid film, as well as quickly switching between 2D and 3D workflows on the LED wall that were used for scene backgrounds.

The production featured creative uses of pre-recorded video plates for scenes involving the “Vertibird'' helicopter. AOIN worked closely with technical partner ioversal to implement their Vertex media server software that acted as a versatile real-time A/V playback production suite that satisfied increasingly complex production requests and demanding budgets.

AOIN was also the first studio to port over an existing Hollywood-sized virtual production from Unreal Engine 4 to 5, which is no small feat. Not only did the team update and reconstruct all the Unreal features used from the first block of shooting, but they also unlocked and streamlined the latest virtual production updates Epic Games was keen on seeing implemented at a volume.
The Result

From a technical standpoint, the stage also saw an impressive 99% screen uptime, a largely unprecedented achievement within the world of virtual production. Any unit production manager will say that consistent uptime is critical to the operation and overall budget of a volume. Fuse Technical Group was pleased to inform All of it Now upon reviewing post-shoot metrics on how they operated their volume that it was likely the most uptime they had ever seen in a production of this scale.

This uptime is informed by reliable tracking data that allows production and post-production crews to complete their work - All of it Now developed several custom tracking validation tools to enforce oversight from many locations around the stage.

These included visualizations of camera positions and stability of incoming tracking data, AR overlays for alignment and accuracy validation over their physical counterparts, as well as virtual-set previsualizations to confirm scenic elements’ locations within the volume during construction. These tools made it quick and efficient to catch and isolate issues on set to cAonfirm if visual anomalies came from the camera, tracking system, server output, or LED panels, and intervene before they became a problem for production.

One notable moment during production that validated the robust toolset developed for the show involved a complex lens swap for a shot on the final episode. In order to achieve a low-angle shot with the heavy film camera mounted on a crane arm inside the volume, the cinematographers chose to use a periscope-lens attachment that would allow them to raise the camera and angle it down, while still capturing a low-angle shot facing up. The interior of the observatory in this scene was a fully built set, which meant the volume operation team had no direct visibility of the camera and had to rely on our tracking tools and the camera feed in order to confirm the data was correct. All of it Now’s operators were able to catch the seemingly erroneous tracking data, deduce what was happening, and apply corrective transforms to the camera frustum before the crew within the volume even radioed back that the lens swap had occurred.

“Fallout” debuted as the most-streamed title of the April 8-14 viewing window and hit the highest viewership ever achieved by a Prime Video title in a single week, and  was watched for 2.9 billion minutes in its first five days of availability, which is more than one billion minutes above the record set by the previous record holder.

projects.summary: For Charity: Water’s annual fundraising gala, All of it Now developed the real-time visual and interactive systems behind the Halo, an 88-foot-diameter LED ring installed at the San Francisco Armory. A bespoke donation platform connected more than 500 tablets to a generative Notch and WebGL system, transforming live fundraising data into visuals displayed across the 14,000-pixel-wide screen.
projects.title: CHARITY: WATER

children.text: For Charity: Water’s annual fundraising gala, All of it Now was brought on to design, program, and operate the 360° visual system for the Halo, an 88-foot-diameter LED ring installed at the San Francisco Armory. The installation combined 360° video supplied by Bodega Studios and Charity: Water partners with generative graphics developed in-house at AOIN, creating a continuous visual environment around the audience.

At the center of the experience was a custom donation platform designed to turn fundraising activity into live visual content. Each guest received a personalized tablet to make a donation, with the data feeding directly into AOIN’s generative graphics system. Names, pledge amounts, and the tangible impact of each donation were visualized on the Halo in real time, allowing the installation to evolve continuously throughout the evening.

The donation system was built to manage more than 500 tablets simultaneously, processing incoming data and driving the generative Totalizer graphics across a display more than 14,000 pixels wide. Notch and WebGL were used together to generate and update the visuals in real time, while a disguise GX2 media server handled playback and output for the 360° LED display.

The system was designed to operate reliably at the scale of a live fundraising event, connecting hundreds of individual interactions to a single shared visual environment. By the end of the evening, the Halo had helped visualize more than $7 million in donations, funding a new water drilling rig and projects serving communities across Ethiopia.

projects.summary: For Michelob ULTRA’s McEnroe vs. McEnroe, a real-time AR system was developed to place virtual versions of John McEnroe across the court alongside his live performance. Unreal Engine, Stype camera tracking, nDisplay, and robotic ball-launch systems were integrated to create a fully interactive physical and virtual tennis match.
projects.title: MCENROE VS MCENROE

children.text: For ESPN’s McEnroe vs McEnroe, Unit9 approached All of it Now with a very special project. In essence, the project was a virtual tennis tournament between tennis legend John McEnroe, playing against younger virtual versions of himself.

Unit9, FCB and Michelob Ultra’s unique project involved a real tennis court constructed on a soundstage in Los Angeles, and combined 3 camera Augmented Reality, nDisplay projection output onto a fog screen, as well as robot arms with tennis ball cannons, all controlled in real-time using Unreal Engine.
AOIN Involvement

AOIN created the technical Unreal infrastructure, building and designing the AR system, managing the Stype camera tracking team, and delivering AR composite feeds to the director in real-time. AOIN also rendered several fully virtual camera angles, animated within UE, and using recorded gameplay elements.

This approach gave Director James Medcraft the freedom to use a combination of clean camera feeds, AR composite feeds and shots of the projected McEnroe Avatar to give the audience a variety of shots that have the authentic look and feel of a professional tennis match.
Technical Challenges
Because the virtual McEnroe needed to serve and return tennis balls back out at real McEnroe, a standard projection screen or LED wall was not an option.

Instead, a transparent “fog screen” was used, and positioned just beyond the net, so that real McEnroe could see the virtual McEnroe, while still allowing the ball to be returned without compromising the ball’s trajectory or speed.

Behind the smoke and mist sat 4 robot arms from the Motorized Precision team, equipped with solenoids which would shoot the balls in different areas of the court to keep McEnroe on his toes. These robots were controlled via the Unreal project, and all 4 arms would work together with the ball machines to simulate a tennis match. On a given point there would be anywhere from eight to 32 return options to spit a ball back out at the real McEnroe.
The Result
This project was a truly unique and dynamic take on virtual humans, and effectively bridged the gap between the physical and virtual worlds with every piece of cutting edge technology available.

With over 10 million views across ESPN’s channels, McEnroe vs McEnroe attracted more eyeballs than the 2021 NBA finals – making this one of the most-watched sports events of the year, winning 5 Cannes Lion Gold awards in 2022.

Our work encompassed both the design and technical integration of the Notch system, taking the looks from creative development through live implementation for the UK tour. The resulting visual package continued beyond the initial UK run, with the Notch camera looks carrying forward into Bad Omens’ US run the following year. This created a flexible real-time visual system that could evolve with the production while maintaining a consistent visual language across the different stages of the tour.

children.text: Linkin Park's From Zero album and tour signify the band's powerful resurgence after nearly eight years of silence. Following the heartbreaking loss of lead vocalist Chester Bennington, this project embodies a fierce revival with a fresh lineup, featuring vocalist Emily Armstrong and drummer Colin Brittain.

The From Zero tour was crafted in three distinct phases: the Launch and Livestream Event, the Arena Tour, and the Stadium Tour. Each phase builds upon the previous, culminating in an expansive, visually stunning experience that captures the band’s redefined sound and vision.
AOIN Involvement

All of it Now (AOIN) was enlisted by frequent collaborator STURDY. to bring this ambitious project to life. STURDY. tasked AOIN with supporting the launch event, Arena shows, and Stadium tours, each presenting unique technical and creative challenges.

With a focus on tight integration across lighting, lasers, and audio, AOIN was the ideal partner to synthesize live camera feeds, MIDI instruments, and timecode inputs, pushing the boundaries of live performance. A range of tools, including Notch, Embergen, and After Effects, were used to craft visually dynamic moments tailored to each show phase.
Technical Challenges

One of the project's biggest challenges was leveraging the newly released Notch 1.0. As is common with major software overhauls, AOIN encountered bugs and roadblocks, but longstanding trust and collaboration between AOIN and Notch helped to overcome these hurdles.

Another technical feat was integrating live data from Joe Hahn’s DJ Pioneer CDJ controller to control Notch effects in real-time, resulting in a distinctive, dynamic focal point that draws audiences directly into the performance.

Following the Arena tour, Linkin Park sought to scale up their production for larger stadium venues. AOIN supported this expansion by reformatting the 360 arena stage design to accommodate a design suited for stadium venues. With the design phase completed, AOIN developed a versatile Notch block that could be adapted not only for the stadium tour but also for future festivals and one off performances, ensuring a seamless visual experience across venues and LED canvases.
The Result:

The From Zero tour has been celebrated by fans and critics alike for its innovative approach to live performance, blending powerful visuals and immersive technology to capture the band’s evolving identity. More than a comeback, the tour is a tribute to Chester Bennington’s legacy, resonating with longtime fans and inviting them to be part of the band's journey forward. Each phase of the tour brings a distinct and unforgettable experience, honoring the past while boldly reimagining the future of Linkin Park.

From camera-driven film strips and real-time fire simulations to UVW-mapped environments and musicality-driven effects, Notch became an active part of the visual system rather than a separate effects layer.
projects.title: MORGAN WALLEN

children.text: For Morgan Wallen’s Still The Problem Tour, All of it Now began development in 2025 and continued through the launch of the 2026 tour, providing ongoing creative and technical support as the production evolved. AOIN’s scope included screens production, real-time Notch integration, and programming, with a particular focus on developing a Notch pipeline that could connect rendered content with live, interactive systems.

Rather than using Notch solely as an effects or playback platform, the system incorporated real-time tracking, simulation, interaction, and camera processing directly into the show’s content pipeline. This allowed live inputs to become part of the rendered environments and gave the visual system greater flexibility to respond to the performance in real time.

Across the production, Notch was used to create camera-driven content as well as augment pre-rendered environments. Live camera feeds became the basis for treatments including film strips and other camera-driven compositions, while real-time fire and environmental simulations could be layered into or behind rendered content. UVW-based workflows extended this integration further, allowing tracked camera feeds to be mapped onto specific surfaces within moving environments. Television screens within rendered scenes, for example, could receive live camera content while maintaining accurate mapping as the surfaces moved through the scene.

The same real-time framework was also used to introduce greater musicality and responsiveness into the visual system, allowing individual elements to react and evolve alongside the performance. By combining rendered assets with live camera, tracking, simulation, and interactive processes, Notch became an extension of the show’s existing content pipeline rather than a separate visual layer.

Development continued through the 2026 tour launch, with the system remaining flexible enough to accommodate creative changes and new technical requirements as the production evolved. The resulting pipeline connected the show’s pre-rendered content with live inputs and real-time processes, creating a more responsive visual system without requiring the production to abandon its existing content workflow.

projects.title: Coldplay ft BTS

children.text: When Coldplay and BTS came together for their 2021 smash single “My Universe”, their musical styles weren’t the only things blended together to achieve something spectacular.
The track’s music video leveraged 3D volumetric capture to record each member from every angle, allowing the supergroups to appear together despite performing from half a world away.
We came in to take this one step further: bridge the gap between worlds by bringing the video’s holograms into the real world through augmented reality (AR).
Why Real-Time

Rather than utilize a pepper’s ghost effect most known from 2Pac’s Coachella “appearance”, combining Dimension Studios’ volumetric capture data with Unreal Engine enabled a real-time workflow offering several advantages over a post-heavy pipeline while preserving a live performance’s energy.

Optimizing for real-time playback with Unreal Engine meant that a full pre-visualization process was possible without any performer digital or otherwise setting foot onstage. Additionally, near-instant adjustments to AR performers’ position and timing could be made on site as well as in post-production.

Volumetric video was similarly critical to our success, capturing every subtlety of the performers for playback without necessitating deep dives into animation pipelines. It also facilitated dynamic camera movements and streamlined post-production by allowing certain shots to be recomposited.
Challenges
As with any disruptive workflow, innovative solutions are needed for persistent problems.
In this case, we needed to devise a method for synchronizing a massive amount of real-time data across multiple cameras in order to maintain the 3D hologram effect.

AOIN consulted with Microsoft to review the volumetric plugin’s source code, which allowed us to add custom functionality necessary to keep each AR performer synchronized to timecode. By dedicating a Silverdraft server for each of seven cameras, directors could follow traditional directing workflows for determining shots to use complete with AR elements.

What’s Next
Our work with The Voice represents a lot of firsts, not least of which is the first time the show incorporated augmented reality into its presentation.

When it comes to production, data throttling issues which held back similar performances can now be overcome. For this project, by using Microsoft’s volumetric technology, we are able to compress large amounts of data into a format that is able to be played back in real-time, while maintaining once-unattainable levels of detail. Because of these advancements, we are now able to bring archival quality volumetric assets into a live broadcast environment.

projects.title: RIOT X ARCANE

children.text: In 2009, fledgling video game startup Riot Games launched its first title: League of Legends. Fast forward by a decade and that very title was celebrating its 10th anniversary, having since  grown into a gaming juggernaut as well as Riot’s tentpole franchise. As part of the festivities, Riot announced an ambitious extension of League of Legends’ universe: an animated series called Arcane to be released through Netflix.
On November 19th, 2021, Riot Games launched its Undercity Nights event in Los Angeles, a once-in-a-lifetime experiential pop-up coinciding with Arcane’s season finale.

A two-day hybrid festival welcomed attendees to Arcane’s undercity of Zaun. Event proceedings featured live League of Legends competition, virtual meet-and-greet opportunities with the show’s voice actors and creators, a concert featuring artists from the soundtrack and more broadcast worldwide.
AOIN Involvement

The event’s broadcast was produced by the BC Live team, who enlisted AOIN to design and integrate a real-time augmented reality environment enveloping home viewers in the setting as much as those attending in person.
These AR set extension elements allowed the practical environment to expand beyond the venue’s physical confines, allowing viewers to gaze into the undercity and soak in the city of Zaun.

To bring this vision to life, AOIN transformed an offline rendering of the undercity into an AR environment optimized for real-time playback. Additionally, the team designed custom holdouts and masking post-process tools for runtime compositing within Unreal Engine.

AOIN worked closely with Stype and BC Live to coordinate a delicate load-in procedure resulting in AR camera accuracy down to the millimeter, a process crucial for sustaining the digital illusion and for ensuring the AR holdout tools worked as expected.
Technical Challenges

One of our primary challenges for this project was developing a custom solution for integrating AR elements into an existing physical set built to emulate the show’s undercity. Arcane viewers were already intimately familiar with the setting, so reproducing Zaun’s look and feel was of the utmost importance.

Onsite AR integration for this project was particularly difficult, as while most of the scenic and production elements were already in place at the time of integration, others were still arriving onsite for showtime. This meant that AOIN needed to develop a custom solution for ensuring AR element accuracy while working around existing production elements and coordinating closely with the core production team to avoid delays and stoppages.
Our Solution

To accommodate this dynamic environment, All of it Now developed a custom AR holdouts tool enabling AR elements to be properly masked and occluded by real-world elements, seamlessly melding the digital and physical worlds into one.

To achieve this, AOIN used 3D models of the fabricated set as masking elements for the AR objects. These masking elements unlocked tremendous creative potential, allowing for a much more dynamic AR environment, spanning far wider and deeper than a traditional AR broadcast would normally accommodate.

Augmented reality elements are typically overlaid on top of the camera feed; it is as if someone had applied a sticker to a camera’s lens. Given the shifting perspective of the camera, a simple composite would severely constrain AR element positioning and create other occlusion issues.
By innovating this holdouts tool, production elements like the lighting rig and camera jib were hidden, preserving the immersive quality of the show’s environment.
The Result

By leveraging existing game assets for integration into the physical set as AR elements and developing the AR holdout occlusion tool, AOIN transported broadcast audiences to Zaun’s streets in all of their grimy glory with an experience exclusively tailored for digital screens.

The broadcast featured the AR elements prominently, using them frequently dramatic camera flythroughs, transitions and as backdrops for segments hosted by the event’s MCs, bringing Arcane fans closer to the show than ever… all without needing to brave the vile stench of the undercity’s air.

projects.title: ENCANTO

children.text: In less than 2 years, Disney’s Encanto has become a cultural phenomenon.

As the first Disney film to reach 200 million streaming hours on Disney+, the first Disney song of the 21st century to top the US Billboard 100, a chart-topping album, and an Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, Encanto‘s success was unprecedented. This success was also in large part due to the hit songs written by Lin-Manuel Miranda and Germaine Franco, including “We Don’t Talk About Bruno”, “The Family Madrigal”, “Surface Pressure” and Oscar-nominated original song “Dos Oruguitas”.

With the runaway success of Encanto, taking the hit songs to the stage was inevitable. And with so much Broadway caliber talent in the original cast including Miranda, Stephanie Beatriz and Olga Merediz, transitioning their performances to the stage was seamless and destined for success.

Due to the film being produced and released during COVID, Encanto at the Hollywood Bowl was the first time that the cast were able to sing together in person. The cast were also never able to attend any press junkets or conventional movie premieres due to the pandemic.
With this in mind, Encanto at the Hollywood Bowl was positioned to be the homecoming and premiere event that the film always deserved.
AOIN Involvement

All of it Now was introduced to the Fulwell 73 team via North House, and worked in close collaboration with the Fulwell 73 and NorthHouse teams to establish a design philosophy and language for the augmented reality (AR) elements. It was quickly determined that the AR elements would best serve as extensions of the projection content, using the vertical space above the Bowl as the creative canvas.

The North House team shared assets used in the projection content, enabling creative cohesion between projection and AR elements. Both teams used Unreal Engine for the creative content, which became a shared collaborative platform across both teams.The 3D meshes of the venue were also used for dynamic occlusion of the AR elements so that AR objects could be placed both in front and behind the bowl and other set elements.

All of it Now worked closely with the Stype team to track and calibrate 4 cameras for use in the live broadcast as well as to record camera tracking data for use in rendering out AR plates, which the post-production team overlaid onto the UHD camera records.
Technical Challenges
The AR content pipeline needed to serve two use cases:
1. Live broadcast AR visible to the audience.
2. A post-production pipeline for the streaming audience on Disney+.
For the live AR component, content needed to be optimized for real-time playback in Unreal 5.03 to then be re-rendered in UHD for the streaming version on Disney+.
With both real-time and post-production workflows requiring seamless and parallel pipelines, Unreal Engine was the natural choice for the project.

children.text: Following All of it Now’s initial collaboration with Production Designer Paul “Arlo” Guthrie on Melanie Martinez’s 2023 Portals Tour, the team continued into the 2024 Trilogy Tour. AOIN handled screens production, Disguise programming, and the development of real-time Notch camera looks integrated with the show’s content and overall visual language.

The production featured a large upstage wall with a projection scrim, paired with automated lifts from TAIT to create a layered stage environment. The show ran on Disguise GX3 media servers supplied by AOIN, housed in a custom touring rack designed and fabricated for the production. The system supported complex Notch treatments, including Notch’s background removal tools within the live camera looks, while Disguise provided a real-time previs environment for visualizing the relationship between the scrim, lifts, and screen content.

A key part of the system was the integration of lift automation data from TAIT Navigator via PSN. The positioning data provided millimeter-level information that could be fed directly into the real-time visual system. For “Class Fight,” the lift's position drove a digital playground seesaw, allowing the graphic to respond directly to the physical movement of the platform. On “Strawberry Shortcake” and “Alphabet Boy,” the same data kept projection content precisely aligned with the moving lifts.

This integration allowed physical stage automation to become an active input to the visual system rather than a separate layer of the production. AOIN carried the workflow from creative development and previs through Disguise programming and live operation, creating a unified system across Notch, projection, media servers, and automated stage elements. The Trilogy Tour ultimately played to more than 375,000 ticketed fans across its reported North American dates before continuing into Europe.

writeupBlocks.text: Melanie Martinez’s Trilogy tour represents the convergence of 3 album cycles that culminates in an epic 3 act journey through nearly every song on each of her three albums - “Cry Baby,” “K-12” and “Portals.”

AOIN Involvement:
All of it Now was first contacted by renowned Production Designer Arlo Guthrie to program her Portals Tour in 2024, with that relationship blooming into the 2024 Trilogy Tour. The tour featured a large upstage wall, with an exceptionally clever use of projection scrim, that added a whole layer of dimensionality to the show, especially when paired with the automation lifts from Tait Towers.
All of it Now created Notch IMAG looks to complement the look and feel of the screen content, which was expertly crafted and created by the team at Normal. In addition to the creative camera treatments, All of it Now also used Notch
The show ran on the disguise gx3’s, which was selected for both creative and technical reasons. The high performance of the gx3 allowed for limitless creative potential in the Notch looks, which featured Notch’s background removal, to great effect. Disguise was also especially useful as a previz tool. Understanding the impact of the scrim on the upstage wall content was crucial, as well as being able to visualize the lift automation data, and the upstage wall as a cohesive creative concept.

Technical Challenges:



Automation data was sent to the servers via Tait Navigator, which sends positional information of the lifts with the Posi-Stage-Net (PSN) protocol. This data provided millimeter level accuracy of the position of the platforms, which ended up driving a number of creative effects in the show.
One of the most impressive generative elements of the show was the use of the lift tracking data for “Class Fight”, in which a playground see-saw receives PSN data, and moves the lift up and down in real time. It was vital for this element to be driven by real time data, so that in the event of a lift failure, or the artist going up on the lift late, the content for the lift was responsive to the real world, rather than keyframed in advance. 
For other songs, like “Strawberry Shortcake”, or “Alphabet Boy”, the lift data was used to drive the projection scrim element, so that the scrim content could be properly lined up to the lift position flawlessly night after night.

The Result:
The tour has been a huge success, with critical acclaim from fans of both her latest work and her earliest work, performing to sold out crowds across 27 US venues, with over 375,000 tickets sold. The tour continues on to Europe in Fall 2024.

children.text: For Peso Pluma’s Éxodo Tour, All of it Now worked alongside STURDY. as a technical and real-time content partner, initially handling screens production and camera design before expanding into the show’s interactive LED floor system. The in-the-round stage required a content pipeline that could support the floor and surrounding screens while incorporating live tracking data from the physical production. The resulting system connected Follow-Me tracking, Posi-Stage-Net (PSN), Notch, and EmberGen across content development, real-time processing, and live playback.

A central component of the system was making the LED floor responsive to the performers moving across it. Follow-Me follow-spot tracking data was fed into Notch, providing real-time positional information that could drive visual responses on the floor. PSN data added another layer of tracking and control, allowing additional stage information to be incorporated into the real-time system. Rather than relying exclusively on pre-rendered or timecoded content, the floor could respond directly to movement and activity within the live production.

Notch was used to build the interactive floor elements and IMAG treatments, translating tracking data into visual responses across the stage. The system supported a range of treatments, from interactive effects tied to performer position to larger compositions spanning the floor and surrounding screens.

Alongside the real-time development, All of it Now created custom 2D and 3D content using EmberGen, including smoke and fire simulations designed around the physical dimensions and contours of the stage. The ability to iterate quickly on simulations allowed the effects to be developed specifically for the production and integrated into the broader Notch and screens pipeline.

The resulting system connected content, tracking, and live processing into a single visual environment, allowing the physical performance to directly influence what appeared on the LED floor. By combining Follow-Me, PSN, Notch, and EmberGen, the production turned the stage itself into an active visual element rather than simply a surface for playback.

projects.title: OUTSIDE LANDS

children.text: The Outside Lands Music and Arts Festival is a masterpiece of city planning and civic engagement with the city of San Francisco.

Nestled within the city’s iconic Golden Gate Park, the weekend’s revelries blend together technology, music, art and gourmet while surrounded by nature to create an experience that can only be described as uniquely San Franciscan.

Following the cancellation of 2020’s edition and last year’s festival taking place abnormally late, 2022 marked the year that Outside Lands roared back at full force, welcoming 225,000 attendees over its customary late August weekend.

It’s no surprise, then, that any brand would want to maintain a long-standing presence at the festival. A titan of the global tech scene born in the Bay Area aspired to invite attendees to celebrate their brand by adding a new element to Outside Lands’ ever-evolving tapestry, and enlisted All of it Now to make it happen.
AOIN Involvement

Our design objective was to create an activation that was closely tied to music, dynamic and kinetic, while still retaining the brand association. Within this objective, the brand wanted to incorporate their signature “Bong” soundmark as a key part of the experience.
All of it Now was contracted to design, fabricate and produce an interactive experience at Outside Lands 2022, achieving these goals over a six-week production period.

The proposed solution was a bespoke rhythm game inspired by the overarching “Spark City” concept, imagining a near-future world where technology has made city living a utopian dream, and encouraging guests to
Do Something Wonderful
™. Spark City was a living, breathing world with a full 24-hour day-night cycle and interactive elements that adapted to each time period.

As users danced to the client-supplied “Bring Back the Bong” track, they triggered interactive elements inspired by the city. During the day, participants produced flying birds, flying cars, blossoming flowers, and spinning windmills; at night, these were replaced with flashing city lights, holographic city signs, fireworks and even a meteor shower.

The game was developed inside of Epic Games’ new Unreal Engine 5.0.3. AOIN made specific use of UE5's new Nanite system as well as its new Lumen lighting features, which allowed for increased visual fidelity as well as stunning day-into-night transitions.
AOIN created the game’s interaction system in TouchDesigner, which enabled development and testing of the environment, visual effects and lighting in parallel with Spark City’s interaction logic.
Beyond software, AOIN was also responsible for the hardware development and in-house fabrication for the footpad triggers and interaction kiosk.

As a bonus feature, the system was able to capture usage metrics, which were analyzed by the AOIN team to determine which visual effects were favored, with the results passed on to the client for further review.
Technical Challenges

One of the biggest challenges facing this project was to design a game that was quick, intuitive and dynamic, while being robust enough to withstand thousands of button presses from a swarm of festival-goers. AOIN rapidly iterated upon the system’s design in collaboration with the client’s team, making careful note of brand guidelines, user interaction flow and real-time graphics performance limitations.

Additionally, designing and developing the game’s interaction hardware within a tight deadline presented its own challenges. By bringing the design, fabrication and programming process in-house, All of it Now produced and implemented a seamless interaction between the digital and physical worlds while meeting the necessary production milestones.
The Result
By the time the curtains fell on Outside Lands 2022, our activation had a staggering number of usages with over 1,500 total games played and 70,000+ hits of the game pad.

At a festival headlined by music luminaries the likes of Green Day, SZA, Post Malone and Phoebe Bridgers, a consistent line of guests waited patiently for their turn to visit Spark City, with competitive players returning to best their previous scores as well as their friends’.

projects.title: ANYMA ÆDEN

children.text: ÆDEN was designed to extend Anyma’s digital world beyond the LED canvas and into the live camera. For the Coachella Main Stage, that meant building an AR system capable of integrating Unreal Engine content into a large-scale live production while maintaining accurate perspective, lighting, and spatial relationships across multiple moving cameras.

The production began with Unreal Engine previsualization and content integration, optimizing the AR assets and animations supplied by ÆTHOS for real-time performance. ÆTHOS handled character development, rigging, and animation, including Beatrix, Anyma’s mech angel character modeled after BLACKPINK’s Lisa. AOIN integrated Beatrix and the additional AR assets into the Unreal environment and developed the systems required to bring them into the live production. When Lisa joined Anyma onstage as a guest performer, Beatrix appeared alongside her as her digital counterpart, creating one of the performance’s defining AR moments.

The system operated across three simultaneously active cameras, including two tripod cameras equipped with STYPE camera tracking and a Spidercam moving dynamically above the audience. Maintaining accurate tracking through the Spidercam’s continuous movement required precise alignment between the Unreal environment, camera perspective, and physical stage. STYPE and StypeLand formed the core of the tracking and compositing pipeline, keeping the digital elements locked to the Main Stage across all three camera perspectives.

DMX data from the lighting system was fed directly into the AR pipeline, allowing virtual elements to follow the same lighting cues as the physical stage. LED content was also used as a lighting source for the AR elements, extending the visual interaction between the screen, virtual characters, and physical environment. Scenic elements were tracked within the AR system and accounted for in the perspective, occlusion, and compositing passes, keeping the virtual and physical spaces precisely aligned.

The production ultimately required two full rounds of on-site integration after severe weather canceled the first Coachella weekend. AOIN returned for the second weekend to rebuild and operate the complete AR system, managing Unreal content, camera tracking, compositing, lighting integration, and live operation throughout the performance. The result was a real-time AR pipeline that extended ÆDEN beyond the physical LED canvas and into the broadcast camera, bringing Anyma’s digital world directly into the live stage environment.
